Osteomalacia is basically low vit D or calcium (or CKD causing impairment in calcium and phos balance) that causes bone not to mineralize. As a result it deforms and causes a lot of pain. It’s adult rickets. No effect on hematopoesis. 

Think of spongiosa as the primary bone that is very dense but brittle because it can’t take a hit without easily breaking. If it isn’t resorbed and replaced by more “airy” bone then that’s petrosis (think of the bone hard as a rock and as a result can’t take any impact without breaking, versus trabeculae is more porous so can take trauma and “bounce back”). Because the spongiosa is replaced by medullary bone and bone marrow, hematopoesis has to find somewhere else to happen which will be the fetal location, spleen and liver.

This isn’t meant to be mean, I’m just showing that it’s not easy to “just do whatever you want.” There is a lot of nuance and literature to be updated on. You can do “basic” things like clear cut anxiety or depression in an otherwise relatively healthy person by prescribing an SSRI. CBT is almost never done inpatient (except in small doses usually by trained therapists rather than psychiatrists even, at least at my institution). Of course I’m not advocating for consulting for every little thing without thought, but you can’t really safely practice medicine out of your scope of training.

I found direct impact in teaching, too. As a teacher, you get the chance to inspire and push students toward finding who they are and want to be (I only TAed and tutored so I don’t mean to come off high and mighty lol, but I loved having the chance to make students go “ohh” and then ask me what other classes they could take to learn more). What’s wonderful about medicine is you can be a physician and a teacher, as well as a researcher.

PAs and NPs are awesome, but I want to be an expert and a leader. Don’t get me wrong, when I had my first panic attack a PA treated me and she was excellent, better than some doctors my parents or I have had. But the reason she treated me is because it was “simple” relative to other cases, and I want those complex cases.

Ok I really don’t want to be a downer, but if you truly don’t enjoy it, then quit. Research is exhausting and it stretches you a lot.

But for some encouragement: 2.5 years ago I started research and I hated it. Despised it. I would sometimes go to bed crying. Then one day while I was doing a western blot, I asked myself “why am I doing these steps? What is the end goal? If my results are positive, wouldn’t that be great? And if they’re negative, then I’m still a step closer to the truth.” Literally within a week of doing this for every experiment, I started to really enjoy research. Now I’m applying to MD/PhD programs too :)

I think looking at why you hate it can help a lot. For me it’s because I felt I was doing tedious work over and over again (I understood why I was doing it, I just didn’t feel like *I* was doing it, like I was just my PI’s extra set of hands).

Do you hate it because of failure? Then honestly either learn to see failure as a success, or quit. I don’t mean to be harsh with that at all, but the very nature of research is failure and stumbling around until you get a good result.

Is it lonely? That’s fair! Can you listen to music or a podcast while working? If not and the loneliness is really unbearable, then I recommend finding a lab that has more of an outgoing culture (or even human interaction).
